cards.q: DNA’s four bases are A, C, G and…
How many chromosomes are in a human body cell?
cards.w: 23 pairs — one of each pair from each parent. 23 is the count in an egg or sperm cell.

cards.q: A variant that shows only when inherited from both parents is…
RNA uses which base in place of thymine?
Who published DNA’s double helix in 1953?
cards.w: Built on Rosalind Franklin’s X-ray images, used without her knowledge.

cards.q: Mendel worked out inheritance by breeding…
Identical twins share…

Where does most nutrient absorption happen?
How many bones does an adult have?
cards.w: Babies start with about 300; many fuse together as they grow.

cards.q: Which part of the brain handles balance?
Red blood cells carry oxygen using…
Natural selection acts on…
Darwin’s finches came from the…
Humans and chimpanzees have…
cards.w: We did not descend from chimps — both lines split from one older species.

cards.q: Whales evolved from…
Same origin, different use — those structures are…
Roughly how old is the Earth?
Birds are the living descendants of…
Antibiotic resistance is an example of…
Which planet is closest to the Sun?
Which planet is hottest?
cards.w: Mercury sits closer, but Venus’s thick CO₂ blanket traps far more heat.

cards.q: How many moons does Mars have?
Which planet has the fastest winds?
The largest planet is…
Demoted from planet to dwarf planet in 2006:
A year on Venus is shorter than…
cards.w: Venus turns so slowly that one rotation takes longer than one trip round the Sun.

cards.q: The asteroid belt sits between…
Our galaxy is the…
cards.k: We live in the Milky Way

cards.q: The Sun is a…
A light year measures…

Most of a galaxy’s visible mass sits in its…
The universe is about…
Which colour of star burns hottest?
cards.w: Backwards from taps and maps: on stars, blue is hot and red is cool.

cards.q: The Great Pyramid at Giza was built for…
Hieroglyphs were deciphered thanks to the…
The first known written law code comes from…
Which empire built Machu Picchu?
Athens is credited with the first…
Alexander the Great was tutored by…
The Colosseum held roughly…
Rome’s republic gave way to empire under…
cards.w: Caesar was never emperor — his heir Augustus took that step.

cards.q: The Berlin Wall fell in…
The first person in space was…
The Second World War ended in…
Apollo 11 landed on the Moon in…
Penicillin was discovered by…
The United Nations was founded in…
cards.w: 1919 was the League of Nations — the attempt that came before.

cards.q: Which country launched the first satellite?
Apartheid in South Africa formally ended in the…
The longest river in the world is the…
cards.w: Contested — by length the Nile leads, but the Amazon carries far more water.

cards.q: Everest sits on the border of Nepal and…
The deepest ocean trench is the…
Which river flows through Paris?
The largest freshwater lake by volume is…
Which continent has no rivers to speak of?
The Andes run along which coast?
The Sahara is roughly the size of…
The capital of Australia is…
The capital of Turkey is…
The capital of Canada is…
The capital of Brazil is…
The capital of Switzerland is…
The capital of New Zealand is…
The capital of Morocco is…
The capital of Myanmar is…
cards.w: Built from scratch and made capital in 2006; Yangon is still much larger.

cards.q: “Salary” comes from the Latin for…
“Quarantine” comes from the Italian for…
“Sandwich” is named after…
“Muscle” comes from the Latin for…
cards.w: A flexing bicep looked, to Roman eyes, like a mouse moving under the skin.

cards.q: “Alcohol” entered English from…
“Robot” was coined in a…
“Avocado” traces back to…
“Nightmare” originally meant a…
cards.w: The “mare” is an old word for a demon that sat on a sleeper’s chest — no horse involved.

cards.q: Turning on its own axis is…
“Affect” is usually a…
With things you can count, use…
“Its” without an apostrophe means…
A “principal” is…
a: A person or the main thing

cards.q: “Literally” strictly means…
“Compliment” with an i means…
Who implies — and who infers?
Most of the Great Wall standing today was built by the…
cards.w: Qin's walls were rammed earth; the stone wall tourists walk is 1,500 years younger.

cards.q: When Cleopatra was born, the Great Pyramid was already…
cards.w: She lived nearer in time to the Moon landing than to the Great Pyramid.

cards.q: The Library of Alexandria was lost…
cards.w: No single fire ended it — funding cuts, wars and neglect did, across centuries.

cards.q: The ancient Olympic Games were held in honour of…
A Roman gladiator fight usually ended…
cards.w: A trained gladiator cost a fortune to keep; killing one threw that money away.

cards.q: Roughly how much of an adult's body weight is water?
At rest, how much of the brain is active?
cards.w: The 10% claim has no source in neuroscience — scans light the whole organ up.

cards.q: Which blood type can donate to anyone?
cards.w: AB positive is the opposite — the universal recipient, not the universal donor.

cards.q: Which organ filters waste out of the blood?
A red blood cell lives for about…
The Titanic sank in…
The Wright brothers first flew in…
cards.w: A decade before WWI made aeroplanes ordinary — earlier than most people place it.

cards.q: The Chernobyl disaster happened in…
cards.w: 1991 is the Soviet collapse — the association that pulls the guess late.

cards.q: India became independent in…
cards.w: 1950 is Republic Day — the constitution, not independence.

cards.q: The first woman to win a Nobel Prize was…
cards.w: Physics, 1903, shared with Pierre and Becquerel. Franklin famously never won — the injustice people remember pulls the guess.

cards.q: The capital of the United States is…
The capital of Vietnam is…
The capital of the Netherlands is…
cards.w: The government sits in The Hague, but the constitution names Amsterdam the capital — the trap catches people who know half the story.

cards.q: The capital of Nigeria is…
cards.w: The capital moved from Lagos to purpose-built Abuja in 1991; Lagos stays the giant.

cards.q: The capital of Tanzania is…
cards.w: Dodoma has been the official capital since 1996; Dar es Salaam remains the largest city and former capital.

cards.q: What controls what enters and leaves a cell?
cards.w: Plant cells have a wall too, but that is rigid support — the membrane underneath is what actually decides what crosses.

cards.q: What speeds a cell's chemical reactions up without being used up?
cards.w: Enzymes lower the energy a reaction needs and come out unchanged, so a tiny amount works over and over.

cards.q: Water moving across a membrane toward the saltier side is…
cards.w: Osmosis is diffusion's special case: the membrane lets water through but not the salt, so the water is what moves.

cards.q: Where does a new cell come from?
cards.w: Virchow's line — omnis cellula e cellula. It is the observation that closed the door on spontaneous generation.

cards.q: Which organelle packages and ships proteins?
cards.w: Ribosomes build the protein; the Golgi folds, tags and sends it on. Building and shipping are different jobs in the same factory.

cards.q: Weather and climate differ because…
cards.w: Climate is weather averaged over about thirty years, which is why one cold week is not evidence about it either way.

cards.q: Standing on the Moon, what actually changes?
cards.w: Mass is how much of you there is; weight is gravity pulling on it. The Moon pulls a sixth as hard.

cards.q: A snake that injects toxin through a bite is…
cards.w: Venom is delivered by a bite or sting; poison is absorbed or swallowed. A pufferfish is poisonous, a cobra is venomous.

cards.q: Comparing two things, you use…
cards.w: Than compares, then sequences. If the sentence would take “next”, it wants then.

cards.q: Antibiotics work against…
cards.w: Antibiotics attack bacterial machinery viruses do not have — which is why they do nothing for a cold.

cards.q: The second-highest mountain on Earth is…
Which river carries the most water?
Kilimanjaro, Africa's highest peak, is a…
The river that carved the Grand Canyon is the…
Which mountains draw the classic Europe–Asia line?
cards.w: The 18th-century convention puts the line on the Urals; the Caucasus marks its disputed southern stretch, which is why it pulls votes.

cards.q: Onboard leftovers from an ancestor — those structures are…
England's peppered moths turned dark because…
Most of life's history on Earth was spent as…
Lucy, the famous fossil, was a…
In biology, "the fittest" is the one that…
How different is your DNA from a stranger's?
cards.w: Any two people are about 99.9% identical — the ~1% figure people reach for is the human-chimp comparison.

cards.q: The first mammal cloned from an adult cell was a…
cards.w: Dolly (1996), grown from a mammary-gland cell — mice, the lab default, weren't cloned until two years later.

cards.q: Roughly how many protein-coding genes do you have?
cards.w: Far fewer than the pre-genome guess of 100,000. The famous 3 billion counts base pairs, not genes.

cards.q: Mitochondrial DNA is inherited from…
cards.w: Sperm mitochondria are destroyed after fertilisation, so the egg's line carries it — the basis of the 'Mitochondrial Eve' idea.

cards.q: A baby's chromosomal sex is settled by…
cards.w: Eggs always carry an X; sperm carry X or Y — history blamed mothers for a coin the father's side flips.

cards.q: “Ketchup” most likely began as a…
cards.w: From a Chinese fermented fish sauce (kê-tsiap); tomatoes joined the recipe centuries later.

cards.q: “Trivia” comes from the Latin for…
cards.w: A trivium was a crossroads — the place where commonplace, everyday talk circulated.

cards.q: A “clue” was originally a…
cards.w: A “clew” of yarn — like the one Theseus unwound to find his way out of the labyrinth.

cards.q: “Disaster” literally means a bad…
cards.w: Dis- plus astrum: born under an unfavourable star, back when the sky took the blame.

cards.q: “Denim” is named after a city in…
cards.w: Serge de Nîmes. Italy is the half-knowledge trap: that city named the jeans — Genoa — not the cloth.

cards.q: Which planet has the most moons?
cards.w: Saturn passed Jupiter in 2023 — well over a hundred confirmed, many just a few kilometres across.

cards.q: The Great Red Spot is…
cards.w: A storm wider than Earth that has been blowing for at least 200 years.

cards.q: Sunlight reaches Earth in about…
Which planet spins on its side?
cards.w: Tilted about 98° — likely knocked over by an ancient collision. Venus is the backwards one, not the sideways one.

cards.q: How much of the solar system's mass is the Sun?
cards.w: 99.8% — Jupiter takes most of the rest, and every other body shares the crumbs.

cards.q: When you look at a distant star, you see it…
cards.w: The light left years — sometimes millennia — ago. Some of those stars no longer exist.

cards.q: What is the Sun mostly made of?
The brightest star in our night sky is…
cards.w: Polaris is famous for holding still, not for brightness — it ranks about 48th. Venus is brighter, but it is a planet.

cards.q: How many stars can you see at once with the naked eye, from a truly dark place?
cards.w: Around 2,500 at once — the Milky Way's glow is the rest, unresolved.

cards.q: What keeps the Sun shining?
cards.w: Hydrogen fusing into helium in the core — not combustion; there is nothing up there to burn.

cards.q: Pompeii was buried by…
cards.w: AD 79 — and the town had already been rattled by a major earthquake seventeen years earlier.

cards.q: The oldest known writing was mostly used for…
cards.w: The earliest cuneiform tablets are inventories — grain, beer, sheep — centuries before anyone wrote a poem down.

cards.q: The Sphinx's missing nose was…
cards.w: Drawings made decades before Napoleon's campaign already show the Sphinx noseless.

cards.q: The pyramids were built mainly by…
cards.w: Workers' villages near Giza show bread and beer rations, medical care and honourable burials — not slave quarters.

cards.q: The trial of Socrates was decided by…
cards.w: Athenian juries ran to hundreds precisely so they could not be bribed.

cards.q: Your stomach gets a new lining every…
cards.w: The acid would digest the stomach itself otherwise — the mucus lining turns over in under a week.

cards.q: The body's strongest muscle for its size is…
cards.w: The masseter — bite force concentrates through a short, brutal lever.

cards.q: Which sense is wired most directly to memory?
cards.w: Olfactory signals skip the brain's relay station and land beside the memory centres — hence the time-travel of a familiar smell.

cards.q: Goosebumps are…
cards.w: The muscles that raise hairs made ancestors look bigger and warmer; the reflex outlived the coat.

cards.q: How many times does your heart beat in a day, roughly?
The first successful heart transplant was performed in…
cards.w: Christiaan Barnard, Groote Schuur Hospital, 1967 — the patient lived eighteen days; the technique lived on.

cards.q: Television was first demonstrated publicly in the…
cards.w: John Logie Baird showed working television in 1926 — two decades before most homes saw one.

cards.q: The Empire State Building went up in about…
cards.w: First steel to opening day in under fourteen months, 1930 to 1931 — Depression labour, round-the-clock shifts.

cards.q: The first email was sent in…
cards.w: Ray Tomlinson sent the first networked email on ARPANET in 1971 — the web came nineteen years later.

cards.q: Concorde crossed the Atlantic in about…
cards.w: London to New York at twice the speed of sound — no airliner has come close since its 2003 retirement.

cards.q: The capital of Pakistan is…
cards.w: Purpose-built in the 1960s to take the government from Karachi — the port kept the size, the new city took the state.

cards.q: The capital of Kazakhstan is…
cards.w: The capital moved north from Almaty in 1997; the city has since been renamed twice — Astana, Nur-Sultan, Astana again.

cards.q: The capital of Ivory Coast is…
cards.w: The official capital since 1983 — the first president's home village, with a basilica bigger than St Peter's; Abidjan kept the ministries.

cards.q: Bolivia's constitutional capital is…
cards.w: Sucre holds the constitutional title and the supreme court; the government sits in La Paz — both answers win arguments.

cards.q: The capital of Sri Lanka is…
cards.w: The legislative capital since 1982, swallowed by greater Colombo — which is why everyone says Colombo.

cards.q: A cell that can still become many different cell types is…
cards.w: Germ cells are the tempting wrong turn — they make eggs and sperm, one committed job. A stem cell is the uncommitted one.

cards.q: Roughly how many cells make up a human body?
cards.k: A body is trillions of cells
cards.w: Best current estimates land near 37 trillion — billions sounds enormous and is off by a factor of a thousand.

cards.q: The jelly that fills a cell, where much of its chemistry runs, is…
cards.w: Plasma is the liquid part of blood — a fluid BETWEEN cells, which is exactly why it reads so plausibly here.

cards.q: Is a virus a cell?
a: No — it has no cell machinery
cards.k: A virus is not a cell
cards.w: A virus is genetic material in a protein coat — no ribosomes, no metabolism. It borrows a real cell's machinery to copy itself.

cards.q: Nerve impulses travel along a cell called a…
cards.w: The near-names are the whole trap: a neutron is a particle, a nephron a kidney unit, a neutrophil a white blood cell.

cards.q: The one growing UP from a cave floor is a…
cards.w: Stalactites hold tight to the ceiling; stalagmites might reach it one day. Where the two meet, cavers call it a column.

cards.q: “e.g.” introduces…
cards.w: Exempli gratia — for the sake of an example. Defining is i.e.'s job (id est, 'that is'), which is exactly the swap.

cards.q: In a pavement, the cement is…
cards.w: Concrete is the finished material — cement plus water, sand and gravel. Calling the slab 'cement' is the everyday slip this pair exists for.

cards.q: The singular of “bacteria” is…
cards.w: A Latin neuter plural, like 'data' and 'media' — the plural form is so common it reads as singular.

cards.q: Wanting what someone else has is, strictly speaking…
cards.w: Jealousy strictly fears losing what you already have; envy covets what you don't. Everyday use blurs them — careful writing keeps the line.

cards.q: The only national flag with more than four sides belongs to…
cards.w: Switzerland and Vatican City are the square ones — still four sides. Nepal’s two stacked pennants make five.

cards.q: The national flag with a rifle on it belongs to…
cards.w: Angola is the near-miss — machete and cog-wheel. Mozambique’s carries an AK-47, crossed with a hoe over a book.

cards.q: Indonesia’s flag is almost identical to…
cards.w: Poland is the flip — white over red. Monaco’s red-over-white differs from Indonesia’s only in proportions.

cards.q: How many stars are on the flag of China?
cards.w: One large star and four small — the big one is what memory keeps, and the trap.

cards.q: The Union Jack combines the crosses of…
cards.k: No Wales in the Union Jack
cards.w: St George, St Andrew and St Patrick — the Welsh dragon never made it in.

cards.q: Which colour appears on the most national flags?
cards.k: Red is the commonest flag colour
cards.w: Roughly three in four national flags carry red; white runs it close, blue further back.

cards.q: The world’s largest island is…
cards.w: Australia is bigger but counts as a continent — the exact line this question exists to draw.

cards.q: The lowest point on Earth’s land surface is the shore of…
cards.w: About 430 m below sea level. Death Valley is North America’s low point, not the world’s.

cards.q: Strictly speaking, the largest desert on Earth is…
cards.w: A desert is defined by precipitation, not sand — and the ice sheet gets almost none.

cards.q: The Volga, Europe’s longest river, empties into…
cards.k: The Volga ends in the Caspian
cards.w: A closed sea — the Volga never reaches the open ocean at all.

cards.q: Roughly when did the dinosaurs (except birds) die out?
cards.w: The asteroid’s boundary layer dates it; each near-miss option is a thousandfold off.

cards.q: Which of these is OLDEST as a group?
cards.w: Sharks swam tens of millions of years before the first true trees stood; grass is younger than T. rex.

cards.q: A trait that spreads because mates prefer it is…
cards.w: Darwin’s second engine: the tail costs survival and pays in mates.

cards.q: Insects and birds both fly. Their wings are…
cards.w: Analogous — same use from separate origins. The mirror of homologous, and the swap everyone makes.

cards.q: What does DNA stand for?
cards.w: The sugar is deoxyribose — the plausible wrong answers all garble that half.

cards.q: The DNA in one of your cells, stretched out, runs about…
cards.k: Two metres of DNA per cell
cards.w: Coiled around histones into a nucleus a hundredth of a millimetre wide.

cards.q: The enzyme that copies DNA is…
cards.w: Ribosomes read RNA into protein — the copying itself is polymerase’s job.

cards.q: Your blood type is inherited from…
cards.w: A and B are co-dominant; two O parents can only make O — the kitchen-table proof.

cards.q: “Companion” literally means someone you share…
cards.w: Latin com + panis. The road answer belongs to “travel”, from travail.

cards.q: “Deadline” began as…
a: A line at a prison camp
cards.w: A Civil-War camp boundary not to be crossed; newspapers took the word, not the stakes.

cards.q: “Vaccine” comes from the Latin for…
cards.w: Vacca — Jenner’s cowpox inoculations named the whole idea.

cards.q: A “freelancer” was originally…
cards.w: Scott’s Ivanhoe popularised it: a lance for hire, loyal to whoever paid.

cards.q: The tallest known volcano in the solar system stands on…
cards.w: Three times Everest — low gravity and no drifting plates let it keep growing in place.

cards.q: Saturn’s rings are mostly…
cards.w: Billions of ice pieces, grains to houses — bright precisely because ice reflects.

cards.q: One day on Mercury, sunrise to sunrise, lasts about…
cards.k: A Mercury day outlasts its year
cards.w: It spins three times for every two orbits — sunrise to sunrise beats its own 88-day year.

cards.q: The Moon is slowly…
cards.w: About 3.8 cm a year — measured by bouncing lasers off Apollo’s mirrors.

cards.q: When the Sun dies, it will…
a: Swell, then fade to an ember
cards.k: The Sun ends as an ember
cards.w: Too light to go supernova — red giant first, then a white dwarf, cooling for eternity.

cards.q: The Milky Way and Andromeda are…
cards.w: Due in about four billion years — stars are so sparse that almost none will collide.

cards.q: A teaspoon of neutron star would weigh about…
cards.w: A city-sized core with the Sun’s mass — what a supernova leaves compressed behind.

cards.q: Stars twinkle because of…
cards.w: Turbulent air bends the light on its way down; from orbit, stars burn steady.

cards.q: A full suit of knight’s plate armour weighed about…
cards.w: About a modern infantry load, spread better. Knights mounted unaided — the crane story is Victorian stagecraft.

cards.q: Viking helmets, as archaeology finds them, were…
cards.w: The horns are 19th-century opera costume — Wagner’s stage, not a battlefield. The one intact find, Gjermundbu, is plain iron.

cards.q: 1066, the Battle of Hastings — who took England?
cards.w: Duke William crossed from Normandy; Harold fell at Hastings. The one date English schooling never lets go of.

cards.q: The Black Death of 1347–1351 killed roughly…
a: A third to half of Europe
cards.k: a third of Europe, or more
cards.w: Estimates run 30–60% of Europe’s population in four years — the deadliest pandemic in the continent’s record.

cards.q: What did educated medieval Europeans think of the Earth’s shape?
cards.w: Columbus’s critics doubted his distances, not the globe. The medieval-flat-earth story was largely invented in the 1800s.

cards.q: Medieval life expectancy was about 35. For adults that meant…
cards.w: Infant mortality drags the average down; a peasant who reached twenty-one could expect decades more.

cards.q: The oldest national flag still in use belongs to…
cards.w: Legend drops it from the sky at Lyndanisse, 1219; the record keeps it in continuous use longer than any other.

cards.q: Two national flags picture their own country’s map: Cyprus and…
cards.w: Both wear their own outline — flags born of disputed borders, drawing the claim itself.

cards.q: Which country flies its flag upside-down to signal war?
cards.w: Blue uppermost in peace, red in war — the only national flag whose orientation is itself a message.

cards.q: The stripes on the US flag count…
cards.w: Stars grew with the states; the stripes froze at the original thirteen colonies.

cards.q: The world’s tallest waterfall, Angel Falls, drops in…
cards.w: 979 metres off the Auyán-tepui plateau — so tall the water mists before it lands.

cards.q: Measured from its base, the tallest mountain on Earth is…
cards.w: Base to summit it tops 10,000 metres; Everest keeps the crown only when you start counting at sea level.

cards.q: The Danube touches more countries than any river. How many?
cards.w: Germany to the Black Sea through or along ten states — no other river borders more.

cards.q: How many bridges cross the Amazon’s main stem?
cards.w: Rainforest offers few roads to join; the one big bridge at Manaus crosses a tributary, the Negro.

cards.q: Evolution works toward ever-more-perfect creatures — true?
a: False — it only fits the present
cards.w: Selection has no foresight; a cave fish losing its eyes is evolution too. Fit means local, not better.

cards.q: The Grants measured Galápagos finch beaks changing in…
cards.w: One drought shifted seed sizes and the island’s beak average within a generation — selection observed, not inferred.

cards.q: Every known living thing shares…
cards.w: The same DNA letters spell a bacterium and you — the strongest single line of evidence for one ancestry.

cards.q: Are humans still evolving?
cards.w: Adult milk digestion spread within the last 10,000 years, alongside dairying — selection running inside recorded history.

cards.q: Do identical twins have identical fingerprints?
a: No — ridges form in the womb
cards.w: Ridge detail sets in womb currents and touch, not in the genome — no two prints repeat, twins included.

cards.q: An onion carries several times your DNA. What does that show?
cards.w: Much DNA is repeats and relics; an onion’s heap outweighs ours without outthinking us. Size is not sophistication.

cards.q: The share of human genes with a counterpart in a banana is roughly…
cards.w: Basic cell machinery is ancient and shared; the often-quoted figure counts genes with a recognisable banana counterpart.

cards.q: Your skin cells and brain cells carry…
cards.w: Nearly every cell holds the full text; cell types differ by which genes are switched on.

cards.q: “Panic” is named after…
cards.w: The god Pan’s shout scattered flocks and armies; groundless, spreading terror kept his name.

cards.q: “Sabotage” traces to sabots, which were…
cards.w: From clumsy-shoe insults to deliberate bungling — the thrown-shoe-in-the-machine story is likely legend, the word real.

cards.q: “Hazard” began as…
cards.w: Arabic al-zahr, the die, became a medieval gambling game, then the risk itself.

cards.q: “Whiskey” comes from a Gaelic phrase meaning…
cards.w: Uisce beatha, water of life — the same idea Latin kept in aqua vitae and Scandinavia in akvavit.

cards.q: Which planet would float in a big-enough bathtub?
cards.w: Its bulk averages lighter than water — the only planet less dense than the tub it would need.

cards.q: The solar system’s planets number…
cards.w: Nine until 2006 — Pluto’s demotion left eight, and the mnemonic lost its pizza.

cards.q: Neptune was discovered by…
cards.w: Uranus’s orbit wobbled; Le Verrier computed the culprit’s position and Berlin found it within a degree, 1846.

cards.q: Which planets have rings?
cards.w: Jupiter, Uranus and Neptune wear faint ones — Saturn’s are just the only rings you can see from a garden.
